learning.javascript:
You already know: going through a string and building a new one

You've already learned how to go through a string one character at a time and build a new string from the pieces (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). In short:

let result = "";
for (const c of s) {
    result += c;   // add c, or something made from it
}

This question adds one thing: changing a letter's case using its character code.

Characters are numbers: ASCII

A computer stores each character as a number, its character code. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is the oldest common set of codes. It uses 0 to 127: 95 printable characters (codes 32 to 126, starting with the space) and 33 invisible control codes (0 to 31, and 127), such as newline (10).

A few landmarks are worth knowing:

  32       space
  48 – 57  '0' to '9'
  65 – 90  'A' to 'Z'
  97 – 122 'a' to 'z'

So 'A' (65) and 'a' (97) are different characters: they're 32 apart. That gap is the same for every letter: 'B' is 66 and 'b' is 98, and so on up to 'Z' (90) and 'z' (122). So adding 32 to an uppercase letter's code gives the matching lowercase letter, and subtracting 32 goes back. Digits and letters are in order, so subtracting codes gives positions: 'c' minus 'a' is 2.

Watch the edges. The characters just outside the letter ranges are not letters: '@' (64), '[' (91), '`' (96) and '{' (123). A range check that's off by one will treat them as letters.

In JavaScript, s.charCodeAt(i) gives the code of the character at index i, and String.fromCharCode(n) goes the other way:

"a".charCodeAt(0);         // 97
String.fromCharCode(65);   // "A"
for (const c of s) { ... } // c is each character of s, as a 1-character string

Beyond ASCII, JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units: charCodeAt returns a number from 0 to 65535, and some characters (such as many emoji) take two units. See MDN's charCodeAt(). That's why this question sticks to ASCII, where one character is always one unit.

ASCII is defined by the standard ANSI X3.4-1986, which ANSI sells rather than publishing free. RFC 20 (1969) is a free primary description of the same code, including the full table.

Solve this one with character codes, as above. A later question covers the language's ready-made helpers for changing case.

chr(65)       # "A"
for c in s:   # c is each character of s, as a 1-character string

You've already learned how to go through a string one character at a time and build a new string from the pieces (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). In short:

It uses 0 to 127: 95 printable characters (codes 32 to 126, starting with the space) and 33 invisible control codes (0 to 31, and 127), such as newline (10).

  48 – 57  '0' to '9'

In C++, a char already is a small integer, so you can use it in arithmetic directly or convert it explicitly:

static_cast<int>('a');   // 97
static_cast<char>(65);   // 'A'
'c' - 'a';                // 2
for (char c : s) { ... }  // c is each character of s

learning.java:
You already know: going through a string and building a new one

You've already learned how to go through a string one character at a time and build a new string from the pieces (see Learned earlier at the bottom of this page). In short:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
    sb.append(c);   // add c, or something made from it
}
sb.toString();

This question adds one thing: changing a letter's case using its character code.

Characters are numbers: ASCII

A computer stores each character as a number, its character code. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is the oldest common set of codes. It uses 0 to 127: 95 printable characters (codes 32 to 126, starting with the space) and 33 invisible control codes (0 to 31, and 127), such as newline (10).

A few landmarks are worth knowing:

  32       space
  48 – 57  '0' to '9'

Watch the edges. The characters just outside the letter ranges are not letters: '@' (64), '[' (91), '`' (96) and '{' (123). A range check that's off by one will treat them as letters.

In Java, s.charAt(i) gives the char at index i. A char is a number underneath, so a cast gives its code:

(int) 'a';                      // 97
(char) 65;                      // 'A'
'c' - 'a';                      // 2
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) { ... }  // c is each character of s

Beyond ASCII, a Java char is a UTF-16 code unit (0 to 65535), and some characters (such as many emoji) take two. This question sticks to ASCII, where one character is always one char.

ASCII is defined by the standard ANSI X3.4-1986, which ANSI sells rather than publishing free. RFC 20 (1969) is a free primary description of the same code, including the full table.

Arithmetic on a char gives an int, so cast back: (char) (c - 32). Without the cast, char d = c - 32; doesn't compile ("possible lossy conversion from int to char").
